claims.text: The two-phase coexistence method in ab initio molecular dynamics can accurately predict melting temperature.
The two-phase coexistence method in ab initio molecular dynamics can accurately predict latent heat.
The two-phase coexistence method in ab initio molecular dynamics can accurately predict volume change at the melting point.
The two-phase coexistence method has a lower computational cost than full thermodynamic integration.
A two-phase coexistence calculation uses a simulation cell containing both solid and liquid phases near the expected melting conditions.
Implementing the two-phase coexistence method permits simultaneous evolution of the solid and liquid phases.
The simulation is conducted at constant pressure near the expected melting point while maintaining a solid-liquid interface.
The solid-liquid interface governs the stability and evolution of the coexisting phases.
Observing the stability and evolution of the solid-liquid interface allows the melting temperature to be extracted.
Observing the solid-liquid interface allows the entropy and enthalpy of fusion to be extracted.
Observing the solid-liquid interface allows the volume change at melting to be extracted.
The two-phase coexistence method bypasses expensive free-energy integration.
Predicted melting properties will agree within an acceptable range with experimental data.
Predicted melting properties will agree within an acceptable range with predictions from more computationally intensive methods.
The accuracy of the method may be limited by finite-size effects.
The accuracy of the method may be limited by simulation duration.
The accuracy of the method may depend on the material system.
Density-functional-theory approximations may prevent exact quantitative agreement.
A deviation greater than 5-10% from both experiment and thermodynamic-integration predictions would falsify the hypothesis.
